system_description.narrative_title: Fragmented security‑economy system: wars, markets and tech rivalry
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order today is an open, tightly coupled system in flux where regional wars (Ukraine, the Iran-related Gulf conflict) and climate shocks propagate through energy and shipping chokepoints to unsettle markets, while great‑power tech and trade rivalry (U.S.–China) and activist economic policy (FX intervention, contested central bank politics) create reinforcing feedbacks. These overlapping processes — military escalation, supply‑chain reconfiguration, monetary and fiscal activism, and migration/climate stresses — interact nonlinearly, producing volatility in commodities, currencies and politics and frequent second‑order crises across regions.
system_description.scope: Major state actors (US, China, Russia, Iran, EU, Japan, India, regional powers), interstate conflicts and maritime chokepoints, global energy and commodity markets, international finance and central‑bank policy, technology and supply‑chain ecosystems, migration and climate stressors, and multilateral institutions and defence alliances.
system_description.super_system: The integrated global political‑economic‑security system (the contemporary international order of states, markets, and transnational institutions).
adjacent_subsystems: Global energy markets & maritime chokepoints (Hormuz, Black Sea)

variables.name: Strait of Hormuz control and diplomacy
variables.description: Iran, the United States, Oman and Gulf states are locked in a high-stakes mix of brinkmanship and talks as Tehran presses for new rules over shipping routes while mediators seek a reopening deal that would reshape naval access and commercial traffic.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine war and European security
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine, backed variably by NATO members and partners, are locked in a grinding conflict marked by intensified drone and long‑range strikes, Russian military reshuffles, dwindling interceptor stocks and mounting pressures on NATO to increase Europe’s own defence capacity.

variables.name: U.S.–China tech and trade rivalry
variables.description: The United States and China are contesting dominance in AI, semiconductors, telecoms and advanced manufacturing through export controls, bans, countermeasures and corporate hedging, shifting supply chains and regulatory regimes worldwide.

variables.name: Global energy supply shocks and reconfiguration
variables.description: A broad set of actors — Gulf producers, Russia, major importers in Europe, China and the United States — are seeing energy flows, stocks and refining capacity reconfigured by military disruptions, export curbs, drought‑strained inland logistics and strategic buying, raising systemic supply and price risks.

variables.name: U.S.–Japan currency activism and global monetary shifts
variables.description: The United States and Japan, through unprecedented FX intervention, Fed leadership choices and divergent central‑bank paths, are driving a new phase of currency and interest‑rate dynamics that is recalibrating global capital flows, bond yields and financial market stress points.
